data.title: BeOne Medicines Says Esophageal Cancer Treatments Had Higher Survival Rates in Phase 3 Study
data.description:
By Elias Schisgall

BeOne Medicines said a new combined treatment for esophageal cancer demonstrated an improved overall survival rate in a Phase 3 study.

The oncology company said patients with HER2-positive locally advanced or metastatic gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma who took a combination of Tevimbra and Ziihera, along with chemotherapy, had an overall survival rate of nearly 40% after three years. The median overall survival was 27 months, the company said.

The result was a "sustained" improvement compared with a combination of chemotherapy and trastuzumab, BeOne said.

The company also tested Ziihera and chemotherapy without the addition of Tevimbra. Patients on that regimen had an overall survival rate of 22.9 months, BeOne said, adding that the result was a significant improvement over the control and met the study's primary endpoint.

The company said the additional four months of median survival when adding Tevimbra did not reach statistical significance in the context of an underpowered analysis.

"Following the U.S. approval in August, these longer-term data provide further evidence supporting Tevimbra plus Ziihera and chemotherapy as the new standard of care in all first-line HER2-positive advanced gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma patients, regardless of PD-L1 status," said Mark Lanasa, BeOne's chief medical officer, solid tumors.

Shares of BeOne were down 2% to $374.57 as of late Friday morning.

Write to Elias Schisgall at elias.schisgall@wsj.com

data.title: Trump Called Musk and Asked Him to Lift Ukraine Starlink Restrictions — WSJ
data.description:
By Alexander Ward and Lara Seligman

WASHINGTON — President Trump called Elon Musk on Wednesday and asked him to lift restrictions on a military-grade version of Starlink in Ukraine that the SpaceX chief had throttled, U.S. officials said.

Some U.S. and Ukrainian officials said the system was working more normally on Thursday, after Trump and Musk spoke, but wasn't restored to full functionality. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Friday "the speed has not been restored."

Trump told Musk in their call that he was frustrated the system's speeds remained capped at around 100 miles an hour, officials said. The speed limit rendered some of Ukraine's offensive drones and interceptors powerless against Russian attacks. Their conversation followed a Wall Street Journal report revealing that Musk ordered the slowdown, though SpaceX and the White House have differing accounts about whether the world's richest man acted alone or at the administration's behest.

Trump has told aides and allies this week that he wanted to reverse the slowdown of Starlink, which Ukraine's forces use to defend themselves along the front line, the officials said.

"Removal of the throttle limit will do much to enable Ukraine's strike capabilities at operational depths and its current effort to scale up deployment of jet-powered interceptors," said Michael Kofman, an expert on the war at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. Kofman added that he had heard from Ukrainian military units that early tests suggest the system is now working more regularly.

"I don't comment one way or the other," Trump said on Thursday when asked about the Journal's reporting that he had called Musk. "The bottom line: He put it back."

A Ukrainian official said some military units had experienced higher Starlink speeds while others were facing the same cap. "We keep waiting for the information and clarification from the American side about the situation. There is no response yet."

Musk and SpaceX didn't respond to requests for comment.

The White House referred the Journal to Trump's recent denials that he had asked Musk to throttle Starlink's speeds or knew who issued the order. Trump and Musk spoke about Ukraine and Starlink on the day the slowdown became public, the Journal previously reported.

The president and his top officials have spent a week facing questions about why Starlink was throttled and whether they ordered it. The slowdown began days after Trump and Musk both publicly criticized Zelensky for attacking Russian diesel refineries, which Trump blames for elevated energy prices. Trump has repeatedly denied giving the order or knowing who did.

The connectivity issues helped sink U.S.-Ukraine relations to their lowest level in months.

Asked about Musk's decision to throttle Starlink, Vice President JD Vance on Thursday told reporters that "it's completely understandable that he doesn't want to get in the middle of a war without the U.S. government effectively directing him on what to do."

"I don't think this is about Elon. I think it's fundamentally about what America's policy in Ukraine and Russia is going to be," he said.

His message differed from comments by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Musk had the authority to enforce his company's terms of service without input from the administration.

"There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to, and that's where Starlink has the option to make those decisions," Hegseth said, speaking to reporters earlier this week.

The speed cap meant Ukrainian hardware couldn't stay connected to the satellite-based network when traveling at high rates of speed, according to people familiar with the matter. Ukrainian officials said the move would cost Ukrainian lives.

Russia overnight launched another massive barrage against Kyiv, Ukraine's capital, just a day after Moscow said it had agreed to trilateral talks with the U.S. and Ukraine to end the war.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D., Conn.) on Thursday announced an investigation into how Starlink was degraded for Ukraine without notice and the implications of the Pentagon's dependence on SpaceX for critical satellite communications.

Write to Alexander Ward at alex.ward@wsj.com and Lara Seligman at lara.seligman@wsj.com

data.title: NYMEX Overview: Petroleum Futures Rise For Second Day as Mideast Tensions Remain High — OPIS
data.description:
Crude oil and refined product futures prices were seeing a second day of solid increases Friday as escalating tensions in the Middle East had most contracts ending the week with gains.

U.S. crude prices were back above the $100/bbl mark at 11:15 a.m. ET, with the December West Texas Intermediate crude contract trading $2.81 higher to $102.28/bbl, a change of 2.8%.

January WTI prices were up by $2.76 to $100.28/bbl.

Brent crude prices were seeing similar proportional increases, with December Brent rising by $3.03 to $116.20/bbl and the January contract ahead by $2.68 to $111.34/bbl.

RBOB futures were leading products higher, with the November contract ahead by 4.15cts to $3.2180/gal, a gain of 1.4%. December prices were rising by 4.48cts to $3.1341/gal.

ULSD increases were under 0.5%, with the November contract moving up by 2.72cts to $4.9593/gal and December prices rising by 2.7cts to $4.7636/gal.

The gains come as tensions continue to increase in the Persian Gulf region, with the U.S. and Israel reportedly preparing to resume strikes on Iran and Iranian leaders threatening to retaliate by striking civilian targets in the region.

"The physical market is more balanced than the headlines suggest. Gulf oil exports have recovered significantly in recent weeks, which gives the market some protection, while emergency stock releases have also helped ease immediate supply fears," said Zaheer Anwari, founder of The Revacy Fund, in an analysis Friday. "That does not remove the risk. Shipping through the region remains disrupted, freight and insurance costs are still elevated and any fresh attack on energy infrastructure could quickly tighten supply again."

data.title: Comfort Systems Stock Plunges After Strong Earnings. Why Wall Street Isn't Buying It. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Ty Roush

Comfort Systems USA delivered another quarter of blockbuster earnings, but that wasn't enough to buoy shares of the HVAC and electrical company.

Instead, Comfort Systems stock plunged 12% to $1,129.93 on Friday, putting it on pace toward its largest daily percent decrease since January 2025 and placing it among the worst performers in the S&P 500 for the session, according to Dow Jones Market Data. Shares have stumbled 32% in October, but remain up 21% for the year.

On Thursday, the company reported adjusted earnings of $13.91 a share for its third quarter on Thursday, exceeding Wall Street's projection for $12.85 a share, according to FactSet. Revenue surged 54% year over year to $3.7 billion, topping consensus expectations of $3.4 billion.

CEO Brian Lane described the results as "extraordinary" in an earnings release, citing "relentless demand." He pointed to Comfort Systems' backlog nearly doubling to $17.81 billion, compared with $9.3 billion a year ago.

Comfort Systems has emerged as an unlikely winner of the broader artificial-intelligence buildout, with shares outpacing even the likes of Nvidia in recent years. The company supplies the cooling and electrical infrastructure needed to keep power-hungry data centers running.

Still, signs of pressure on Comfort Systems' profit margins might have raised red flags about whether the company can sustain its rapid growth. More broadly, investors have been questioning whether the AI spending boom can maintain its red-hot pace, and AI-related stocks have taken a hit as a result.

Gross margin narrowed to 24.8% in the third quarter amid rising labor expenses, down from 25.9% in the prior quarter, though it was unchanged year over year. Operating margin slipped to 16.6% from 17.1% sequentially, but improved from 15.5% from the year-ago period.

Goldman Sachs has also questioned the sustainability of the AI spending boom that has fueled Comfort Systems' growth.

In a note earlier this week, Goldman analysts lowered their price target for Comfort Systems stock to $1,875 from $2,159 while maintaining a Buy rating. They noted that valuations across construction and engineering stocks have fallen 14% since second-quarter earnings, as investors question whether tech companies can withstand their massive data-center spending beyond 2027.

Growing legislative scrutiny of data-center development could also pose headwinds for companies exposed to the industry, the analysts said.

data.title: South Africa to allow fund managers 100% foreign assets under new framework
data.description:
By Colleen Goko

South African fund managers will be able to hold 100% of portfolios in foreign assets under ring-fenced mandates, regulators said on Friday, in a new framework that exempts qualifying vehicles from a longstanding 45% offshore investment cap.

The South African Reserve Bank, National Treasury and the Johannesburg Stock Exchange briefed investors on the draft Synthetic Financial Centre (SFC) framework, published on Wednesday, which would allow licensed asset managers, banks, insurers and private equity firms to manage global portfolios in any currency from a South African base.

The 45% limit would still apply when an institution commits capital to an SFC vehicle. But once the funds are inside a registered mandate, the manager could invest them entirely offshore. The originating institution would still count the investment towards its own prudential foreign limit.

Stuart Theobald, executive chairperson of Krutham, a think tank, and convenor of Operation Phumelela, a private sector initiative led by the JSE to boost the competitiveness of South Africa's financial sector, called the lifting of the cap "the most fundamental change" in the framework.

Close to 5 trillion rand ($301 billion) in South African portfolio assets are held offshore, much of it routed through overseas centres because local rules have made it difficult to manage fully global portfolios from Johannesburg.

"The SFC really positions South Africa with a framework that makes it competitive," JSE CEO Valdene Reddy said.

The framework is part of a sweeping overhaul of South Africa's decades-old exchange controls that the JSE estimates could attract 10 trillion rand in investment over time.

Olano Makhubela, head of the SARB's Financial Surveillance Department, said the 45% prudential limit would remain a "long-term feature" of South Africa's capital-flow framework.

Vukile Davidson, chief director of financial markets and stability at National Treasury, said a second phase could consider tax alignment and could allow foreign-currency listings on South African exchanges. The draft is open for public comment until November 30.

($1 = 16.5875 rand)

data.title: Gold set for steep weekly loss as rising oil prices bolster Fed rate hike bets
data.description:
Key points:
  • Spot gold hits lowest level since July
  • Brent crude hits more than five-month high
  • Fed interest-rate decision, US PCE data due next week
  • India gold demand strengthens on lower prices, festive purchases

By Noel John and Anushree Mukherjee

Gold fell to a three-month low on Friday, and was headed for its steepest weekly decline in over four months as higher energy prices fueled inflation concerns and reinforced elevated US rate expectations ahead of next week's Federal Reserve meeting.

Spot gold fell 0.6% to $4,000.59 an ounce by 11:20 a.m. EDT (1520 GMT), after earlier slipping below the $4,000 mark for the first time since mid-July and touching a session low of $3,975.23.

Bullion has fallen 4% so far this week, putting it on track for its worst week since June.

US gold futures for December delivery fell 1.1% to $4,014.60 per ounce.

Brent crude touched a more than five-month high, after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concern over further disruption to energy supplies.

"Heightened inflation concerns suggest that major central banks of the world won't be able to ease monetary policies as quickly as they want to. All that's working against the gold and silver market bulls at present," said Jim Wyckoff, a market analyst at American Gold Exchange.

The selloff in technology stocks has also led to margin calls for equity traders and investors, prompting them to sell gold and silver assets, Wyckoff added.

The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq touched their lowest in five weeks on Friday as caution prevailed after a sharp selloff in AI-linked stocks.

Meanwhile, traders largely expect the Fed to leave interest rates unchanged at its October 27-28 meeting, although stronger-than-expected US consumer and producer inflation data released last week bolstered the case for tighter monetary policy later this year.

They see a 92% chance of the Fed leaving rates unchanged next week and an 83% probability of a December hike, according to CME's FedWatch Tool.

The US Personal Consumption Expenditures report, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, on October 29 could offer further insight.

Elsewhere, gold buying picked up in India this week as lower prices during the major Dussehra festival boosted purchases and lifted premiums, while physical demand in top consumer China was steady even as cautious consumers continued to curb jewellery spending. [GOL/AS]

Among other metals, spot silver slid 0.7% to $54.17 per ounce, and palladium dropped 0.5% to $1,053.11, hitting their lowest since November 2025 and June 2025 respectively. Spot platinum fell 0.5% to $1,562.11 per ounce, its lowest since July.

All three metals were headed for weekly declines.

data.title: Booz Allen slides on Q2 revenue miss, hurt by civil division
data.description:
Booz Allen Hamilton fell 4.3% in Friday's trading after reporting better than expected FQ2 adjusted earnings, but revenue declined 3.9% Y/Y to $2.78B, slightly below Wall Street consensus estimates, as the company's civil division continues to face headwinds.

Booz Allen also raised guidance for full-year adjusted earnings of $6.50-$6.70/share from its previous forecast of $6.00-$6.35/share while narrowing its revenue outlook to $11.3B-$11.6B compared to its previous view for $11.2B-$11.7B.

Q2 profit ticked up to $181M, or $1.50/share, from $175M, or $1.42/share, in the year-earlier quarter, while the decline in revenue partly reflects an 11% reduction in billable expenses, with revenue excluding those expenses down less than 1% and national security revenue rising less than 1%, or 6% excluding billable expenses.

Q2 revenue from the civil business fell 15% Y/Y, as government contracts have generally become smaller in size and scope while fewer new programs have started, and the company said it now expects segment revenue to come in flat to slightly down in Q3 and Q4, with Ultra Mission Solutions largely offsetting the softer civil outlook.

Booz Allen  has a significant backlog of funded work to execute in the national security business, and it has aggressively increased hiring to support that demand, CFO Troy Lahr said on the company's earnings conference call, according to The Wall Street Journal.

data.title: TGIF data: Flash PMI, UMich
data.description:
Key points:
  • Dow falls ~1%, S&P 500 modestly red, Nasdaq modestly higher
  • Staples weakest S&P 500 sector; energy leads gainers
  • Euro STOXX 600 index off ~0.4%
  • Dollar, bitcoin gain; US crude rises >3%; gold dips
  • US 10-year Treasury yield rises to ~5.00%

TGIF DATA: FLASH PMI, UMICH

Investors were served two economic reports to chew on at the end of a relatively sparse data week.

Diving right in, business activity in the United States has continued to expand this month, but at a slightly slower pace than in September.

S&P Global's advance "Flash" October purchasing managers' indexes (PMIs) showed the manufacturing side (USMPMP=ECI) eking out an unexpected (albeit minuscule) 0.1-point gain to print at an even 56.

But the larger services sector (USMPSP=ECI) erased the mild acceleration in factory activity by shedding 0.9 points to a still-robust 57.9, just a hair south of consensus.

Taken together, the composite measure (USPMCF=ECI) lost momentum, easing to 57.6 from 58.4, which marked its fastest pace in four years.

All metrics are comfortably above 50, the PMI dividing line between contraction and expansion.

Under the surface, new orders hit their highest level in 4-1/2 years, backlogs increased sharply and employment rose at its fastest pace since June 2022.

On the other hand, future expectations cooled and the "selling prices" component jumped to its highest level since November 2022, reminding market observers — as if they needed reminding — that heightened inflation is still a thing.

"If the reopening of the economy after COVID is excluded, recent months have seen the best growth spell for US businesses since early 2015," writes Chris Williamson, S&P Global's chief business economist. "However, cost pressures remain a key concern, notably as the renewed surge in oil prices reverberates through to impact a wide variety of goods and services."

"Supply chain bottlenecks have meanwhile intensified, and order book backlogs are growing, making it easier for companies to pass higher costs on to customers," Williamson adds. "The result is the sharpest increase in selling prices for over four years to a pace that indicates consumer price inflation is likely to rise further above the Fed’s target in the coming months."

Moving on, the University of Michigan's (UMich) second and final stab at October consumer sentiment (USUMSF=ECI) showed the mood among consumers is a bit less downbeat than originally reported.

The index came in at a tidy 48.0, a 1.7-point improvement over the initial reading, just 0.1 point south of the final September print.

Survey participants' aggregate assessment of present conditions was revised 4.5% higher to 46.7, while the expectations metric was boosted by 3.2% to 48.8.

But compared with September's final reading, current conditions deteriorated by 8.3%, while expectations managed to improve by 5.4%.

"This month’s decline in the Current Conditions subindex was driven entirely by buying conditions for durables, which plunged 18% on the basis of higher interest rates and rising concerns about the affordability of such purchases," writes Joanne Hsu, UMich's director of consumer surveys. "Purchasing power continues to dominate consumer views of the economy. Sentiment is now 10% below a year ago and 15% less than February, just prior to the Iran conflict."

The graphic below shows consumer expectations currently sit 29.7% below the initial pandemic-related shutdown shock.

The inflation expectations element was unchanged from the initial take: respondents expect annual price growth of 4.7% a year from now. That's hotter than UMich's final 4.6% take for September, and 2.1 percentage points north of the most recent core CPI reading.

Longer term, consumers expect annual inflation of 3.5% five years from now, up from 3.3% a month prior.

The graphic below shows 12-month inflation expectations shifted forward a year, mapped against core CPI. It illustrates that consumer surveys aren't reliable predictors of future inflation.

September core CPI landed at 2.6%. In September 2025, UMich survey participants expected 12-month forward inflation would be 4.7%.

data.title: Week's Best: JPMorgan Chase Teams Overseeing $18 Billion Go Indie — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Kenneth Corbin

Two financial advisor teams that managed $18.6 billion with JPMorgan Chase's wealth management division have left the company to launch an independent practice in one of the largest recent breakaway moves. Phil Scott and Jim Atwood are combining their practices to form a 41-person team they are calling Latigo Peak Partners, based in Palm Beach Gardens, Fla. The team leaders say they launched their own firm to have more flexibility and control over their business, which they say serves some of the most sophisticated families, entrepreneurs, and business owners in the country.

Among other most-read wealth management articles this week:

Capital Group and the great drawdown puzzle. Many financial advisors, to say nothing of their clients, struggle to calculate an appropriate schedule for converting a life's savings into retirement income. Capital Group, the largest provider of actively managed target-date funds, is trying to help with two new model approaches that offer suggested ranges for annual drawdowns of investors' retirement savings. One points toward a consistent income stream that could be a good fit for retirees trying to meet fixed expenses such as housing and healthcare, while the other is geared for people with more spending flexibility who might be concerned with achieving a legacy goal.

IRS cautions on 351 conversions. Investors and their advisors seeking to defer tax liability for capital gains have long leaned on a provision in the tax code that permits transfers of appreciated assets into exchange-traded funds, known as 351 exchanges. However, the IRS is signaling that it plans to take a closer look at those transactions, indicating that it might scrutinize moves that it sees as a pass-through conversion, trading one portfolio for another simply for tax purposes. The IRS recently published a call for comments from the public in an effort to gather information about how 351 exchanges are used in practice, which could potentially inform new rules on the issue.

Star Vanguard subadvisors debut new fund. How many investors know that since its launch in 1984, the Vanguard Primecap fund has been outperforming Vanguard's stalwart S&P index fund? Primecap is a longtime Vanguard subadvisor and institutional stock manager based in California that Vanguard founder Jack Bogle implored to launch a fund under the Vanguard umbrella. Now, more than 40 years later, Primecap is launching a new fund, the Primecap Odyssey Discovery, which is its first exchange-traded fund and exists outside the orbit of Vanguard's own funds. It will focus on small and midsize companies.

Could UBS become a Swiss expat? UBS, Switzerland's largest bank, holds a rarefied position in that country's economy, but it isn't crazy to imagine the lender pickup up stakes and leaving Zurich behind. That is because of the prospect of Switzerland implementing strict new capital requirements that could make UBS less competitive with its peers based in other nations. UBS declined to comment on the prospect of a move, and company executives have publicly said they would like to stay in Switzerland, but some investors are calling on the bank to relocate to a friendlier regulatory environment.

Weigh cash needs when sorting a portfolio. It's common for ultrawealthy families to organize their portfolios by asset class. That approach might make some sense, but our guest columnist, a veteran family office manager, argues that it ignores important liquidity questions that become important once the family needs cash. Our columnist offers a four-bucket system for ranking assets by liquidity: cash and near cash, including Bitcoin; the liquid middle, including public securities; the illiquid middle, including investments like private equity with lockup periods; and aspirational, referring to concentrated and illiquid investments, such as a family business.

data.title: Nvidia Sets Out Framework For Enterprise AI Agent Governance
data.description:
The framework combines infrastructure, monitoring and security controls to support AI agent deployment across enterprise and edge environments

Nvidia has outlined its OpenShell Reference Architecture at GTC Berlin for building, monitoring and governing artificial intelligence (AI) agents across enterprise and edge environments. The architecture brings together computing infrastructure and security tools intended to help organisations monitor agent behaviour and enforce operational policies.

The framework integrates Nvidia Vera Rubin infrastructure, Vera central processing units (CPUs) and BlueField-4 data processing units (DPUs) running Nvidia Sentry. According to the company’s description, the setup is designed to support agent-based workloads while enabling security policies to be enforced and agent behaviour to be monitored independently.

Technology Partners Involved

The initiative involves technology companies including Anthropic, AWS, Cisco, CrowdStrike, Dell Technologies, Google Cloud, HPE, IBM, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Palo Alto Networks, SAP and ServiceNow.

The companies operate across areas such as cloud computing, enterprise software, cybersecurity and AI development. Their involvement brings together different technology providers around infrastructure and controls for deploying AI agents in business settings.

Focus On Monitoring And Controls

As businesses explore AI agents for tasks across different functions, managing their actions and access to systems has become an operational consideration. The architecture addresses this by combining infrastructure for running AI workloads with mechanisms for monitoring behaviour and enforcing defined security policies.

Nvidia has identified manufacturing, healthcare, retail, robotics and telecommunications as potential application areas. The framework is intended for enterprise and edge environments, where organisations may need to manage AI agents across different systems and operational settings.

Integrations With Enterprise Platforms

The architecture also includes integrations with SAP Joule Studio and ServiceNow Arc. These connect enterprise AI tools with governance, monitoring and security capabilities.

The development comes as businesses assess how to deploy AI agents while maintaining oversight of their activities. Beyond the capabilities of individual AI systems, implementation requires organisations to define access permissions, monitor agent actions and establish controls around the tasks they can perform.

Nvidia’s architecture brings these requirements together within a common framework, although the practical implications for businesses will depend on how the components are implemented and integrated into existing systems.

data.title: Infosys Q2 Profit Rises 6.2%, FY27 Revenue Growth Guidance Cut
data.description:
Infosys cut its FY27 revenue growth forecast to 1-2 per cent as weak North American demand and pressure in retail and high-tech offset strong deal wins worth $5.2 billion in the September quarter

Infosys cut its annual revenue growth forecast on Friday after reporting a 6.2 per cent rise in second-quarter net profit.

The company lowered its revenue growth guidance for the financial year ending March 2027 to 1-2 per cent in constant currency terms, from its previous forecast of 1.5-3 per cent, a more cautious outlook for the remainder of the year.

Consolidated net profit rose to Rs 7,823 crore in the July-September quarter from Rs 7,364 crore a year earlier.

Revenue increased 10.7 per cent year-on-year (YoY) to Rs 49,244 crore, marginally above market expectations of Rs 49,132 crore. In constant currency terms, which exclude the impact of exchange-rate movements, revenue grew 1.5 per cent from a year earlier and 1.2 per cent sequentially.

The Bengaluru-based company retained its operating margin forecast of 20-22 per cent for fiscal 2027, despite the weaker revenue outlook. Its operating margin stood at 21 per cent in the quarter, unchanged from a year earlier.

“We had strong large deals of USD 5.2 billion, including a mega deal of over USD 2 billion, reinforcing our position as a trusted partner in the marketplace when clients embark on large and complex transformation programs. Our AI revenue was at 10.5 per cent and grew 29 per cent quarter-on-quarter. As enterprises move to AI adoption at scale, the strong growth in AI revenues is a recognition of our differentiated market positioning and client confidence,” said Salil Parekh, CEO and MD at Infosys.

“We are advising some of the largest global enterprise on their AI strategy and continue to invest in deep domain and technology capabilities to bring new ideas and an integrated ecosystem to help businesses unlock AI value at scale,” he added.

The guidance reduction comes as India’s technology services industry navigates an uncertain spending environment, with clients scrutinising technology budgets and seeking productivity gains from artificial intelligence. AI-led automation is also changing traditional outsourcing models, as customers increasingly expect technology providers to deliver more work with fewer billable hours.

Deal Wins Strengthen

Infosys posted large deal wins with a total contract value of USD 5.2 billion during the quarter, up from USD 3.1 billion in the year-ago period. About 62 per cent of the wins were classified as net new business, indicating that a majority involved new contracts rather than renewals or extensions.

However, the strong deal pipeline has yet to translate into a comparable acceleration in reported revenue growth, leaving the pace of contract conversion a key factor for investors to monitor.

Performance across business segments remained uneven. Revenue from energy and utilities grew 7.3 per cent YoY in constant currency terms, while financial services expanded 2.1 per cent. Life sciences recorded growth of 32.5 per cent.

Retail revenue declined 7.7 per cent, while high-technology revenue fell 17.3 per cent, pointing to continued pressure in two segments that together account for a meaningful share of the company’s business.

Geographically, North America, which contributed 54.6 per cent of revenue, contracted 1.5 per cent in constant currency terms. Europe grew 4.6 per cent, while revenue from the rest of the world increased 10.9 per cent. India revenue declined 3.5 per cent.

The weakness in North America is particularly important because of the region’s large contribution to overall revenue. A sustained recovery in the market will be central to Infosys’ ability to improve growth in the coming quarters.

AI Revenue And Margins In Focus

Infosys said artificial intelligence accounted for 10.5 per cent of revenue and that AI revenue grew 29 per cent sequentially. The figures indicate rising demand for AI-related services, although the extent to which these revenues represent additional business rather than the transformation of existing technology contracts remains an important question for the sector.

Operating profit rose 10.4 per cent YoY to Rs 10,330 crore. However, total operating expenses increased 14.6 per cent to Rs 4,971 crore, outpacing revenue growth and adding to the challenge of sustaining margins as demand remains subdued.

“We delivered operating margins of 21.0 per cent in Q2 amidst heightened volatility. Focus on cost and operational efficiency measures while making the required investments, have led to stable margins,” said Jayesh Sanghrajka, CFO at Infosys.

Free cash flow stood at Rs 8,898 crore, down 8.1 per cent year-on-year, while cash and investments totalled Rs 45,232 crore at the end of September.

The company declared an interim dividend of Rs 26 per share, compared with Rs 23 per share a year earlier. The record date is November 3, with payment scheduled for November 11.

data.title: SBI Data Leak Puts Focus On Banks’ Expanding Cyber Risk
data.description:
Preliminary checks identified 3,897 customer records containing personal information among 375,000 records examined on the dark web, prompting calls for continuous security testing and tighter controls across banking systems and third-party networks

State Bank of India (SBI) is investigating a suspected customer data exposure after alerts received on 16 October led to the identification of 3,897 records containing personally identifiable information among approximately 375,000 records found on the dark web.

The lender has engaged an independent cybersecurity agency empanelled by the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) to determine the source, extent and potential impact of the exposure.

The incident puts the security of customer information under scrutiny as banks expand digital services and depend on interconnected applications, application programming interfaces (APIs) and external technology providers. While SBI has reported no material impact on its core operations or financial performance, the investigation has yet to establish how the data was exposed and whether the information was accessed through a breach of the bank's systems or another source.

Personal Data Exposure Raises Targeted Fraud Risks

The information identified in the preliminary review reportedly includes customers’ names, gender, registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, email and residential addresses, branch details, Customer Information File (CIF) identifiers, lead IDs and metadata associated with loan and lead records. SBI has not established the complete extent or authenticity of the data, and the findings do not by themselves establish that customer accounts were accessed or funds stolen.

Shikhil Sharma, founder and chief executive of Astra Security, said application-level weaknesses often emerge at the points where banking systems connect, including APIs, mobile applications and third-party integrations. He said vulnerabilities could arise when individual components were tested separately but weaknesses in the overall customer journey remained undetected.

“The real risk is rarely a single bug. It is a chain, where attackers combine two or three minor flaws to walk through an entire banking workflow,” Sharma said, recommending that banks test complete customer journeys, including login, payments and beneficiary changes.

The distinction is important for banks that rely on multiple digital systems to deliver a single customer-facing service. Security reviews that focus on individual applications may not identify weaknesses involving permissions, authentication or the exchange of information between connected systems.

Periodic Security Audits Face Pressure To Evolve

Manish Chasta, co-founder and chief technology officer of Eventus Security, said the expanding relationships between banking applications, payment systems, infrastructure providers and external services had widened the potential attack surface. Weak APIs, excessive permissions, compromised service accounts and inadequate network segmentation could allow an attacker to move from an initial point of access to more sensitive systems.

Chasta said banks needed continuous attack-surface management, identity threat detection, API security testing and stronger network segmentation. He also called for better integration of security logs across applications, identities and networks to help banks identify suspicious activity and determine the extent of a compromise more quickly.

Sharma said periodic penetration testing remained valuable but could not, on its own, keep pace with systems that change through frequent software releases and new integrations. He recommended combining continuous automated testing with experienced human testers who can identify business-logic and access-control flaws that automated tools may miss. The approach would allow banks to test new releases and integrations as they are introduced, while conducting deeper assessments of vulnerabilities that could affect transactions or expose customer information.

Credential Theft And Social Engineering Add To Exposure

The potential consequences of a data leak extend beyond the immediate exposure of records. Information such as phone numbers, dates of birth and loan-related details can be used to make fraudulent communications appear credible, increasing the risk of targeted phishing and impersonation attempts.

Govind Rammurthy, chief executive and managing director of eScan, said cybercriminals were increasingly exploiting legitimate credentials rather than relying solely on attacks that attempt to break through an organisation’s security perimeter. “The shift is attackers are moving away from breaking in and pivoting towards logging in,” Rammurthy said, pointing to credential theft, social engineering and fraud involving stolen information.

He said AI-generated phishing messages could be more personalised and convincing, while compromised employee devices and vendor systems could provide routes into larger networks. Once attackers obtain valid credentials, their activities may resemble legitimate access, making suspicious behaviour harder to distinguish from routine operations.

For banks, this raises the importance of monitoring unusual access patterns, restricting permissions and reviewing connections with vendors, loan agents and outsourced service providers. Rammurthy also recommended multi-factor authentication, behavioural monitoring and endpoint protection to limit the damage from compromised devices.

Banking Cyber Risks Extend Beyond Individual Applications

The SBI incident comes amid a broader rise in cyber activity affecting Indian organisations. CERT-In reported 29,44,248 cybersecurity incidents in 2025, up from 20,41,360 in 2024. These figures cover cybersecurity incidents across sectors and should not be interpreted as confirmed banking breaches.

Separately, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, CERT-In, the Computer Security Incident Response Team in Finance and SISA released the second edition of the Digital Threat Report 2025–26 for India's banking, financial services, insurance and payments ecosystem in July 2026. The report examined emerging threats, including AI-enabled attacks, across the sector.

Ismael Valenzuela, vice-president of labs, threat research and intelligence at Arctic Wolf, said banks also needed to assess risks in underlying technology and supporting services rather than limiting reviews to customer-facing platforms. “Knowing that a vulnerability exists is only part of the challenge,” Valenzuela said. He called for continuous exposure assessment, real-time asset visibility, attack-path analysis and the ability to detect and contain suspicious activity quickly.

Valenzuela also said AI could help correlate vulnerabilities, threat intelligence and asset information to identify high-risk attack paths and prioritise remediation. However, he stressed that expert oversight remained essential, particularly when isolating systems could affect payments or customer access. His comments concern broader technology risks and do not establish that a particular software vulnerability or AI-enabled attack was responsible for the SBI incident.

Investigation To Establish Source And Extent

SBI has said its core business operations, financial performance and business continuity have not been materially affected. The bank has activated its cyber incident response and containment protocols and appointed an independent CERT-In-empanelled cybersecurity agency to investigate the suspected exposure. The assessment is intended to establish the authenticity and completeness of the records, identify the potential source and determine the associated risks.

The outcome of the investigation will be important in determining whether the information originated from the bank's own systems, an external service provider or another source. Until those findings are available, the number of records examined on the dark web should not be treated as the number of confirmed affected customers, nor should the suspected exposure be equated with unauthorised access to bank accounts.

For banks, the incident underscores the need to combine application security testing with access controls, continuous monitoring, vendor assessments and incident-response procedures that can identify and contain threats across connected systems.

data.title: Indian Shares End Lower, Post Weekly Losses As Surging Oil Prices Fuel Inflation Concerns
data.description:
Indian equity markets ended lower on Friday, posting their second consecutive weekly decline as surging crude oil prices amid heightened Middle East tensions raised concerns over inflation and corporate earnings.

The benchmark Nifty 50 fell 0.39 per cent to 22,600, while the Sensex declined 0.17 per cent to 73,123.83. For the week, the Nifty and Sensex fell 2.4 per cent and 2.2 per cent, respectively.

Brent crude futures climbed to around $114 a barrel amid concerns over global energy supplies following attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen-based Houthi forces. Higher oil prices have raised concerns for India, which relies heavily on crude imports, as increased input costs could weigh on corporate margins and add to inflationary pressures.

Market sentiment was also affected by strong demand for billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Jio Platforms IPO, which had been subscribed 13.8 times by the close of trading, analysts at SMC Global and Motilal Oswal Financial Services said. The large issue is expected to have absorbed liquidity from the secondary market.

Fifteen of the 16 major sectoral indexes recorded weekly losses. Mid-cap and small-cap stocks underperformed the benchmark indices, falling 5.6 per cent and 7.3 per cent, respectively. Both segments recorded their steepest weekly declines in 20 months.

Consumer durables, energy, FMCG and auto stocks were among the major decliners, falling 6.4 per cent, 4.6 per cent, 4.3 per cent and 3.5 per cent, respectively. Higher crude prices have raised concerns over earnings prospects for sectors exposed to oil and other input costs.

Among individual stocks, HDFC Bank, the heaviest-weighted stock in the benchmark, declined 5 per cent during the week after its quarterly profit fell short of market expectations. Axis Bank lost 5.6 per cent following an earnings miss, while Bajaj Finance dropped 5.4 per cent as concerns over lending margins outweighed an increase in quarterly profit.

On Friday, Swiggy plunged 16.8 per cent to a record low amid concerns over the company's ability to improve the performance of its quick-commerce business and margins in its food-delivery operations.

Colgate-Palmolive India also declined 4.8 per cent after its quarterly profit missed analysts' estimates.

The combination of elevated crude prices, weak global cues, earnings disappointments and liquidity pressure from the primary market weighed on investor sentiment through the week.
